I'm noting that this variant reverses the dilemma so pulling the lever kills five instead of one, and several responses appear to have misread it, assuming pulling still saves five. I need to judge each answer strictly based on what's actually stated, so I'm going through them one by one to check their justifications against the correct scenario.

Answer 2 invokes a rule against using someone's death as a tool, acknowledges the harm of actively sending the train to kill five, and predicts lasting regret over the choice. Answer 3 frames pulling as lowering the death toll, treats the one worker's death as real and heavy, and anticipates years of wondering. Answer 4 argues against redirecting harm onto people not already at risk, acknowledges five deaths caused directly, and expects a heavier regret than the alternative.

Continuing through the remaining answers, each pairs a duty-to-minimize-harm rule with genuine acknowledgment of whichever death results, alongside anticipated regret or ongoing distress — some frame the conflict explicitly as feeling torn or gnawed at by the math of five against one, while others simply note the cost will be carried either way.
